open_obligations: Check whether Hase et al. observed SGR above 100% in any setting.
Note that Sun et al.'s oracle is 'all levels', not 'hard only'.
Check whether the objection applies only with RL training.
in.other_title: No PGR or SGR analogue because easy-only training can beat full training
in.rationale: Hase et al. define Supervision Gap Recovered with hard-data finetuning as the 100% reference. Sun et al. decline to define an SGR or PGR analogue because models trained only on easier tasks, particularly with RL, sometimes outperform those trained on all levels, which would push such metrics above 100%; Sun et al. use MATH with reward models and RL, Hase et al. ICL, linear probes and QLoRA.
in.scope: proposed CHALLENGES: whether a gap-recovered metric with a hard-data oracle as upper bound is suitable for easy-to-hard evaluation

open_obligations: Check that Hase et al.'s SGR uses training on hard data as the ceiling, so that exceeding it would break the metric
Check how often easy-only training actually exceeds full training in Sun et al.'s tables
in.other_title: Sun et al. decline Hase et al.'s SGR metric because easy-only training can beat full training
in.rationale: The authors argue the SGR-style metric is limited in their setting because its ceiling can be exceeded, a critique of the metric's applicability without a direct conflict with Hase et al.'s findings, so CRITIQUES. Hase et al. study mostly multiple-choice tasks with ICL and SFT, not RL with reward models.
in.scope: proposed CRITIQUES: Whether a supervision-gap-recovered metric anchored on hard-data training is meaningful; holds where easy-only training can exceed the hard-data ceiling

text: The authors define Supervision Gap Recovered as (Easy - Unsupervised) / (Hard - Unsupervised), where Easy, Hard and Unsupervised are hard-test performance after finetuning on easy data, on hard data, or on no data (zero-shot). SGR is 100% when easy data is as effective as hard data and 0% when the easy-finetuned model is no better than zero-shot prompting.
title: Supervision Gap Recovered (SGR) metric for easy-to-hard generalization
